strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: text-to-video generation with an alpha channel. This is practically useful for editing, compositing, games, stickers, and visual effects, where transparent video assets are valuable.

The proposed system is simple and deployment-friendly. Encoding alpha into the RGB latent space, using decoder LoRAs plus a DiT DoRA, avoids the doubled inference cost of approaches such as TransPixeler and appears compatible with existing Wan acceleration tooling.

The manuscript gives a clear high-level description of the VAE design, rendering losses, data sources, captioning process, and inference setup. The qualitative examples show convincing cases for semi-transparent effects, glow, hair, glass, flames, and other difficult alpha-aware content.

The comparison to both open and closed TransPixeler variants is relevant, and the reported runtime gap is substantial: 128 seconds for 81 frames at 480x832 versus 32 minutes for 49 frames at 480x720 for the open TransPixeler implementation on the same device.
The authors acknowledge meaningful failure modes, including unintended background debris and inaccurate alpha masks with holes or semi-transparent regions.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is too qualitative for the strength of the claims. The paper repeatedly claims superiority in visual quality, motion realism, semantic alignment, and transparency rendering, but provides no quantitative metrics, user study, alpha accuracy measures, temporal consistency measures, or standardized benchmark evaluation.

The comparison protocol is not fully controlled. Wan-Alpha uses expanded Chinese prompts with style, shot-size, and transparent-background tags, while TransPixeler examples appear to use much shorter prompts. This makes it hard to isolate model quality from prompt engineering and multilingual/prompt-extension effects.

There are no ablations for the central technical choices: feature merge block design, causal 3D modules, hard/soft rendering losses, Sobel/perceptual losses, decoder LoRA rank, DoRA versus LoRA, dataset filtering, Chinese manual captions, or 4-step LightX2V inference. As a result, the contribution of each component is unclear.

The text-to-video training set is very small, only 437 samples, with 116 Internet videos and manually refined captions. The paper argues that careful curation compensates for scale, but does not provide sufficient evidence about generalization, memorization, train/test separation, or diversity beyond selected examples.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says the released model is available on the website, but the shown manuscript has a blank website field. Important implementation details such as optimizer, learning rates, training hardware, DoRA insertion points, LightX2V settings, prompt extension details, and exact dataset filtering criteria are missing.

The technical novelty is moderate rather than strong. Much of the system combines known ingredients: Wan, LayerDiffuse-style alpha-in-RGB latent representation, LoRA/DoRA adaptation, rectified-flow training, and curated data. The practical integration is useful, but the paper does not deeply analyze why the proposed VAE representation succeeds for video.

The limitations section is brief and does not quantify failure frequency or characterize difficult cases systematically. This matters because alpha artifacts are central to the task and can severely affect downstream compositing usefulness.

strengths: Addresses a useful and underexplored problem: text-to-video generation with an alpha channel, which has clear practical relevance for editing, games, stickers, and compositing workflows.

The proposed system is simple and deployment-oriented: adapting Wan with an alpha-aware VAE, decoder LoRAs, and a DiT DoRA is plausibly more efficient than methods that duplicate the full backbone, and the reported inference-time comparison against TransPixeler-open is a meaningful practical advantage.

The manuscript identifies important data issues for RGBA video generation and makes a reasonable effort to curate higher-quality training examples with manual caption refinement, including semi-transparent objects, glow effects, hair, glass, liquid, and other alpha-sensitive cases.
Qualitative examples suggest the method can generate visually appealing transparent videos in some challenging categories, especially compared with the shown TransPixeler outputs.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is very weak for the strength of the claims. The paper relies almost entirely on qualitative figures, with no quantitative evaluation of RGB quality, alpha accuracy, temporal consistency, text alignment, user preference, matting quality, or compositing artifacts.

The comparison protocol appears unfair or at least insufficiently controlled. Baselines are often prompted with very short prompts, while Wan-Alpha uses longer prompts with added style, shot-size, and transparent-background tags; the model is also tested with Chinese prompts while English translations are shown. This makes it hard to attribute improvements to the method rather than prompt engineering or base-model differences.

There are no ablations for the central design choices: feature merge block, causal 3D modules, hard/soft rendering losses, edge/perceptual losses, decoder LoRA ranks, DoRA vs LoRA, prompt labels, LightX2V acceleration, or dataset curation. As a result, the paper does not establish which components are necessary.

The text-to-video training set is extremely small, only 437 samples, and the paper does not convincingly show generalization beyond the curated prompt styles and object categories. Many examples appear close to the described training distribution, raising concern that results may reflect narrow adaptation rather than robust RGBA video generation.

The VAE is a major claimed contribution, but it is not evaluated independently. There are no reconstruction metrics, alpha-mask metrics, temporal flicker measurements, comparisons to LayerDiffuse/AlphaVAE-style adaptations, or visual analyses of failure modes under compositing.

The method's novelty is limited. Much of the system combines existing ingredients: Wan, LayerDiffuse-style latent transparency, LoRA/DoRA, rectified flow training, LightX2V, and curated data. The paper's contribution is mostly an engineering adaptation, but the experimental support is not strong enough to compensate.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The website/model link is blank in the manuscript, dataset sources include unspecified Internet videos, training details omit optimizer, learning rates, schedules, hardware, preprocessing specifics, augmentation details, and exact inference settings, and the manually refined Chinese captions/labels are not provided.

Limitations are underdeveloped. The paper acknowledges unintended background elements and inaccurate alpha masks, but does not measure their frequency, diagnose causes, or discuss safety/licensing issues around Internet-sourced data.

Presentation has several polish issues, including formatting errors, missing release URL, awkward equation notation, and overconfident language such as 'superior performance' without adequate controlled evidence. These are secondary to the evaluation weaknesses but reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored practical problem: text-to-video generation with an alpha channel. The application value for editing, games, stickers, VFX, and compositing is clear, and the work is well motivated relative to RGB-only video generators and prior transparent image/video methods.

The proposed design is pragmatic and technically sensible. Encoding alpha into the RGB latent space via a Wan-based VAE, using a feature merge block, decoder LoRAs, and a DiT DoRA keeps inference close to the base model and avoids the doubled-backbone cost of TransPixeler. This is a meaningful systems contribution even if several components build on existing ideas.

The qualitative results are strong. Across the shown comparisons, Wan-Alpha generally produces sharper and more coherent objects than TransPixeler, with notably better examples for birds, dragons, candles, hair, glass/water, glow effects, and semi-transparent materials.

Efficiency is a compelling part of the contribution. The claimed comparison against the open TransPixeler implementation is substantial: 81 frames at 480x832 and 16 FPS in 128 seconds versus 49 frames at 480x720 and 8 FPS in 32 minutes on the same device. The lightweight adapter-style deployment is potentially useful for real adoption.

The paper provides useful implementation detail about architecture, losses, training data sources, crop/frame settings, LoRA/DoRA ranks, training iterations, and inference setup. The authors also acknowledge real failure modes such as unintended background debris and alpha-mask holes.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is much narrower than the strength of the claims. There are no quantitative metrics for alpha quality, temporal consistency, prompt alignment, image/video quality, or user preference, and no table summarizing performance. The central claims of superior visual quality, motion realism, and transparency rendering are supported almost entirely by selected qualitative figures.

There are no ablations isolating the contributions of the VAE design, feature merge block, causal 3D modules, hard/soft rendering losses, Sobel/perceptual losses, DoRA versus LoRA, data curation, prompt extension, or LightX2V acceleration. As a result, it is difficult to know which parts are necessary and which gains come mainly from using Wan plus a curated dataset.

The comparison protocol raises fairness concerns. The baseline prompts and Wan-Alpha prompts are not identical; Wan-Alpha often uses richer prompts, style tags, shot-size tags, translated Chinese prompts, and sometimes prompt extension. This makes it hard to attribute quality differences purely to the model rather than prompt engineering or base-model differences.

The text-to-video training set is very small: 437 samples, including only 301 videos from video matting datasets, 20 images, and 116 internet special-effects videos. The paper argues that curation compensates for scale, but without held-out quantitative evaluation or diversity analysis, generalization remains uncertain.

Reproducibility is incomplete as written. The abstract says the released model is available on a website, but the manuscript shows a blank placeholder. Data from additional internet sources is not described in enough detail, and captions are manually refined in Chinese without a released protocol or enough examples to reproduce the dataset construction.

The novelty is moderate rather than fundamental. The work adapts known ideas from LayerDiffuse/AlphaVAE-style latent alpha encoding, LoRA/DoRA adaptation, rectified flow training, and Wan/LightX2V infrastructure to transparent video generation. The integration appears useful, but the paper does not establish a deeper algorithmic advance through analysis or ablation.

The paper would benefit from a more rigorous benchmark setup: fixed prompt sets, identical prompt handling across baselines where possible, evaluation against more transparent-video and layer-aware methods, runtime measured under clearly specified hardware/settings, and direct alpha-channel metrics on held-out RGBA videos.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: text-to-video generation with an alpha channel. Stable RGB-A video generation has clear practical value for design, VFX, games, UI assets, and content creation, and the paper gives a well-motivated account of why directly adapting RGB video models or RGB-A image methods is insufficient.

The proposed system is practically appealing. It preserves the pretrained Wan2.1 text-to-video backbone, adds an RGB-A VAE with separate RGB/alpha decoding via LoRA, and introduces a transparency-guided mean sampler that can be used at inference for approximate control over transparency location and shape. The reported inference efficiency relative to TransPixeler is a notable practical advantage if the comparison is fair.

The paper contributes a curated RGB-A video dataset and describes both VAE training data and generation fine-tuning data. Given the scarcity of high-quality RGB-A video assets, this dataset contribution could be useful to the community if released as promised.

The experimental section compares against the main available RGB-A video generation baselines, including TransPixeler, LayerFlow, LayerDiffuse+AnimateDiff, and a Wan+MatAnyone pipeline. The reported quantitative metrics and user rankings consistently favor the proposed method, and the qualitative figures show visually plausible improvements in hair, glass, smoke/light effects, and transparent backgrounds.

The ablations address the main proposed components: rendering losses, the transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss, and the mean sampler. These ablations provide some evidence that the VAE design and sampler improve reconstruction, transparency behavior, and controllability.
weaknesses: There are concerning technical ambiguities in the formulation. The transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss is written as M multiplied by the RF loss, with M = -1 in non-opaque regions. This appears to make the objective maximize a squared prediction error in transparent regions, potentially yielding an unbounded or unstable optimization unless constrained by omitted implementation details. The manuscript does not adequately justify why this objective is well-posed or how it avoids degenerate solutions.

The rectified-flow equations for the mean sampler appear inconsistent. With Z_t = t * epsilon_tilde + (1 - t) * Z, the velocity target should follow the derivative direction epsilon_tilde - Z, but Eq. 13 defines the target as Z_t - epsilon_tilde. This may be a typo, but it is central enough that it undermines confidence in the exact method being evaluated and reproduced.

The evaluation does not isolate the contribution of the proposed method from the very strong Wan2.1-T2V-14B backbone, LightX2V acceleration, and the curated dataset. Some baselines use different or weaker model foundations, and there is no strong controlled baseline such as Wan2.1 with the same RGB-A VAE but without TABD/MS, Wan2.1 plus conventional alpha conditioning, or a matched architecture trained with standard augmentations/objectives.

Transparency evaluation is weak. The automatic metrics are computed after rendering to a white background and therefore mostly measure RGB/video quality rather than alpha correctness. The user study is important but underspecified: the number of users, prompts/videos, randomization, statistical significance, and annotation interface are not reported in the main paper. This makes the central claim of better transparency less rigorously supported.

The generation fine-tuning dataset is very small, with only 429 samples, and the paper does not sufficiently analyze generalization beyond the demonstrated examples. It is unclear how robust the model is to complex multi-object scenes, multiple transparent objects, unusual alpha topology, non-elliptical object layouts, occlusions, or prompts far outside the curated data distribution.

The Gaussian ellipse mask is a useful control mechanism but also a limitation. It provides only coarse single-ellipse spatial guidance and may be poorly matched to multi-component, thin, concave, or irregular transparent structures. The paper shows a few examples but does not quantify controllability accuracy or failure modes.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the main manuscript. Several important details are deferred to supplementary material, including optimization settings and likely training/evaluation protocols. Dataset collection from Internet sources is mentioned without enough licensing, filtering, or deduplication detail. The model and dataset are promised for release but not available within the reviewed manuscript.

The claims are sometimes stronger than the evidence. The paper says the framework validates stable, controllable transparency generation and superior performance across metrics, but the support is based on a small set of baselines, limited metrics, and qualitative examples. The work is promising, but the current evidence does not fully establish broad robustness or state-of-the-art superiority across the RGB-A video generation problem.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and underexplored problem: text-to-video generation with alpha channels for transparent and semi-transparent content. This is relevant for creative production workflows such as stickers, UI assets, games, and compositing.

The proposed system is practically motivated and reasonably clear at a high level: adapt a strong pretrained RGB video model, train an RGB-A VAE, add transparency-aware losses, and use a mean-shifted noise prior to guide transparent regions.

The paper includes comparisons against the small set of available RGB-A video baselines, including TransPixeler, LayerFlow, LayerDiffuse+AnimateDiff, and a Wan+MatAnyone pipeline. Qualitative examples suggest the method can generate visually appealing transparent videos.

The ablations on rendering losses, the bidirectional diffusion loss, and the mean sampler are helpful and show that the proposed components affect reconstruction quality and transparency placement/control.

The dataset construction effort is a positive contribution, especially because RGB-A video data is scarce and the paper attempts to include semi-transparent effects such as smoke, water, glow, glass, and fabric.
weaknesses: There are serious technical correctness concerns in the formulation. The transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss is defined as M * L_RF with M = -1 in non-opaque regions, which appears to make the optimization maximize a squared diffusion loss in those regions. This could make the objective unbounded or unstable unless additional implementation details constrain it, but the paper does not explain this. Similarly, the modified rectified-flow velocity in Eq. 13 is written as Z_t - epsilon, which does not match the derivative of the interpolation Z_t = t epsilon + (1-t)Z. These issues undermine confidence in the method as specified.

The evaluation is weak for the central claim of transparent video generation. The quantitative metrics in Table 1 mostly assess rendered RGB video quality, aesthetics, text alignment, smoothness, and flicker after compositing onto a white background; they do not directly measure alpha accuracy, semi-transparency fidelity, boundary quality, or temporal alpha consistency. The only transparency-specific evidence is a user ranking study, but the paper does not report the number of users, number of prompts, protocol details, statistical significance, or inter-rater reliability.

The training data for the generation model appears very small: the final RGB-A video generation dataset contains only 429 samples, including only 301 videos from matting datasets plus 85 internet special-effects videos and 43 images. Given that the method adapts a 14B Wan model, the paper does not convincingly separate the contribution of the proposed losses from the strength and priors of the pretrained generator, nor does it demonstrate robust generalization beyond curated examples.

The comparison protocol is not fully convincing. Baselines are heterogeneous and may not be tuned equivalently, while the proposed method benefits from a very strong Wan2.1-T2V-14B backbone, custom curated data, DoRA adaptation, LightX2V acceleration, and alpha-specific processing. The fairness of comparisons against TransPixeler, LayerFlow, and LayerDiffuse+AnimateDiff is not sufficiently analyzed.

The claim of preserving RGB quality while shifting only alpha is not well substantiated. The paper asserts distribution separation but provides no latent-space analysis, likelihood analysis, or diagnostic showing that RGB latents are preserved and alpha latents are shifted in the intended way. The reported VAE reconstruction gains are small and do not directly validate the distribution-learning story.

Reproducibility is limited. Important details are deferred to supplementary material or omitted, including exact data filtering, internet data provenance, prompt sets, user-study design, training schedules beyond iteration counts, loss weights if any, optimizer settings, mask edge cases, and how alpha regions are categorized into opaque/semi-transparent/transparent for the bidirectional loss.

The computational claims are somewhat overstated. The method says it introduces no extra computational cost because LoRA/DoRA can be merged, but inference still requires duplicated VAE decoding for RGB and alpha and custom noise/mask handling. The runtime comparison to TransPixeler is useful but insufficiently controlled across hardware, sampling settings, resolution, frame count, and model size.

The paper's novelty is moderate. Mean-shifted diffusion/noise priors, LoRA/DoRA adaptation, VAE reconstruction/rendering losses, and alpha/video matting datasets are all built from existing ingredients. The combination is practical, but the manuscript does not make a sufficiently rigorous case that the proposed formulation is a principled or technically sound advance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: text-to-video generation with an explicit alpha channel. This is practically useful for compositing, design, games, and video effects, and the manuscript makes a clear case that naive RGB video generation plus matting is not an adequate substitute, especially for semi-transparent effects.

The core idea is sensible and fairly original for this setting: improve RGB-A generation by acting at both ends of the diffusion process, with a VAE objective intended to make RGB and alpha latents more distinguishable and a shifted-noise sampler that gives coarse control over transparent regions. The design is well aligned with the stated failure mode of RGB/alpha entanglement.

The method is efficient relative to backbone-duplication approaches such as TransPixeler: it keeps the base RGB video model largely intact, uses VAE decoder LoRAs and DiT DoRA, and claims mergeable adapters with little inference overhead. This is a useful engineering contribution if released as described.

The experimental section compares against the most relevant available RGB-A video baselines, including LayerFlow, LayerDiffuse+AnimateDiff, open and closed TransPixeler, and a Wan+MatAnyone pipeline. The reported results consistently favor the proposed method across text alignment, aesthetics, naturalness, motion smoothness, temporal flickering, and a user ranking for transparency and overall quality.

The ablations are useful: Table 3 isolates rendering losses and the transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss for VAE reconstruction, while Figures 7-9 qualitatively examine the contribution of TABD, the mean sampler, and the controllability of the Gaussian ellipse mask.

The dataset effort is a strength. The authors aggregate many matting image/video sources, build a large VAE training split, and curate a smaller RGB-A generation dataset emphasizing motion, semi-transparent objects, lighting effects, captions, and labels. This is valuable for a task where data scarcity is a real bottleneck.
weaknesses: The main quantitative evaluation still only indirectly measures the central claim of correct alpha/transparency. VBench and GPT-4o/VLLM scores are computed after rendering onto a white background, so they can miss alpha-channel errors. The only direct transparency evaluation is a user ranking, but the manuscript does not report the number of users, number of prompts/videos, randomization protocol, statistical significance, or whether users saw videos or selected frames.

The proposed bidirectional diffusion loss is under-justified technically. Defining Lbidiff = M * LRF with M = -1 in semi-transparent/transparent regions means the objective can become negative and, if minimized literally, encourages increasing the RF loss in those regions. The paper motivates this as decreasing likelihood of alpha, but does not provide a stability argument, bounded formulation, weighting scheme, or empirical evidence that it does not simply damage transparent-region representations.

There are some mathematical and notation issues that affect clarity and reproducibility. For example, Eq. 13 defines the modified velocity as vt = Zt - eps_tilde, whereas Eq. 2 uses vt = eps - Z for rectified flow; these are not equivalent and the intended convention is unclear. The symbol mu is also overloaded for both the ellipse center and the mean-shift strength. The text/figure descriptions alternate between shifting transparent regions and masks based on opaque point sets, which makes implementation details ambiguous.

The generation dataset appears very small for adapting a 14B video model: only 429 samples are used for RGB-A video generation training, with 1,750 DiT iterations. The results may be impressive, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze generalization beyond the curated data distribution, especially to complex multi-object scenes, unusual transparency layouts, non-human/non-matting-style content, or prompts requiring both opaque and multiple semi-transparent objects.

The comparisons are helpful but not fully controlled. The proposed method uses Wan2.1-T2V-14B as a strong base model, while some baselines, such as AnimateDiff with LayerDiffuse, may be much weaker as video generators. It is therefore difficult to separate gains from the proposed RGB-A learning strategy versus gains from the stronger underlying video model and training recipe.

The ablation evidence is somewhat narrow. Table 3 evaluates VAE reconstruction metrics, but these do not directly establish that TABD improves generative alpha quality. The DiT/mean-sampler ablations are mainly qualitative; there is no quantitative ablation on transparency correctness, controllability accuracy, RGB quality preservation, or computational cost.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete in the manuscript. The authors state that the model and dataset will be open-source, but the website field is blank in the abstract, and many implementation details are deferred to supplementary material that is not available here. Important missing details include prompt/test set construction, user-study protocol, exact training data filtering, loss weights, optimizer settings, and baseline implementation settings.
